title: Kirishima's last night
pull: Sent to shell an airfield, sunk instead

facts.text: Kirishima was one of the oldest big ships in the Japanese fleet. A Kongo class battlecruiser built by Mitsubishi at Nagasaki, she was commissioned on 19 April 1915 and later rebuilt as a fast battleship.
In December 1941 she sailed with the carrier force that attacked Pearl Harbor.
On the night of 12 to 13 November 1942 she and her sister ship Hiei tried to shell Henderson Field on Guadalcanal. Hiei was crippled in a close range night battle and sank; Kirishima got away.

Admiral Yamamoto ordered Vice Admiral Nobutake Kondo to try again on the night of 14 to 15 November. Kondo built a force around Kirishima, with the heavy cruisers Atago and Takao, two light cruisers and nine destroyers. The aim was to knock out the airfield so a troop convoy could land.
Near midnight Kirishima and the cruisers found the US battleship South Dakota and hit her again and again. They did not see USS Washington, which was tracking them by radar in the dark.
Washington opened fire at about 8,400 yards. Within minutes Kirishima took at least nine 16 inch shells, perhaps as many as 20, and dozens of 5 inch hits. Sources disagree on the count.
Her forward turrets were knocked out, fires spread through the ship, and a hit jammed her rudders, leaving her steaming in circles as water poured in.
Her crew fought the flooding for hours while destroyers stood by. At about 03:25 on 15 November she capsized northwest of Savo Island.
212 of her men died. The destroyers Asagumo, Teruzuki and Samidare rescued about 1,100 survivors, among them her captain, Sanji Iwabuchi.

Kondo's bombardment never happened. Of the 11 transports in the convoy, 7 had been sunk by aircraft on 14 November; the last 4 ran aground at Tassafaronga and were destroyed after dawn. Only 2,000 to 3,000 troops got ashore.
It was Japan's last big attempt to retake Guadalcanal by sea. On 31 December 1942 Imperial General Headquarters decided to evacuate the island.

photoNote: Kirishima at anchor in Tsukumo Bay, Japan, 10 May 1937, broadside, in her rebuilt fast battleship form (as she looked at Guadalcanal). Photo by Shizuo Fukui, from the Kure Maritime Museum album (Todaka, Japanese Naval Warship Photo Album: Battleships and Battle Cruisers, p. 124). Commons tags it public domain under PD-Japan (Japanese photo taken before 1946); the page lacks an explicit US PD tag, which Commons flags. Downloaded 1920 px wide. Alternative with an explicit US PD tag: Kirishima at Kure (dated 1930 on the page, file name says 1940), also Fukui, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kirishima_Kure_1940.jpg , shows the older pre 1934 look. Clean US Navy option but tiny: NH 50903, off Amoy 1938, 888 px (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Japanese_battleship_Kirishima.jpg).
photoCredit: Battleship Kirishima at Tsukumo Bay, Japan, 10 May 1937. Photo by Shizuo Fukui, Kure Maritime Museum collection, public domain.

declassified.fact: Kirishima's captain, Sanji Iwabuchi, survived the sinking. In February 1945 he commanded the Japanese naval troops in Manila and refused orders to withdraw, a stand his biography links to his shame over losing his ship. The battle for the city killed about 100,000 Filipino civilians, and Iwabuchi died there.

body:
She had sailed with the carriers that struck Pearl Harbor. Eleven months later, Kirishima was sunk by a ship her crew never saw.

15 November 1942. Vice Admiral Nobutake Kondo took Kirishima toward Guadalcanal to shell Henderson Field, so a Japanese troop convoy could land. Near midnight her guns found the battleship South Dakota and hit her again and again.

Then USS Washington, tracking her by radar from the dark, opened fire. A hit jammed Kirishima's rudders, and she steamed in circles as water poured in. Her crew fought the flooding for hours before she capsized northwest of Savo Island at about 03:25.

212 of her men died. Destroyers picked up about 1,100, among them her captain, Sanji Iwabuchi. The bombardment never came.
